chapters.title: Chapter 5: Markets and the Wider Economy

lessons.title: FIIs, DIIs and Mutual Funds: Who Actually Moves Indian Markets

children.text: Prices move because someone bought and someone sold. That obvious point is worth taking seriously, because the identity of those buyers and sellers explains most large market moves far better than any narrative about sentiment. Four groups do almost all of the trading in Indian equities, and each behaves in a predictable way.

markDefs.definition: Foreign Portfolio Investors: overseas funds registered with SEBI to invest in Indian securities. The older term FII is still used interchangeably in news coverage.
Domestic Institutional Investors: Indian mutual funds, insurance companies, pension funds and banks investing in Indian securities.

children.text: . Alongside them sit retail investors, buying directly, and promoters, who mostly hold rather than trade. Daily flow data for the first two is published, which is why news channels quote it constantly.

body.caption: Who Trades Indian Equities, and Why

cells: FPIs, also called FIIs
Global funds, pension funds and hedge funds registered with SEBI
Global interest rates, dollar strength, how India looks against other emerging markets
Move in large, correlated blocks; can sell heavily for reasons unrelated to India
Domestic mutual funds
AMCs deploying money from SIPs and lump sum investments
Inflows from investors, which arrive steadily every month
Often buy when foreigners sell, because fresh money keeps arriving
Insurers and pension funds
Life insurers, EPFO, NPS fund managers
Long-term liabilities and mandated allocation rules
Slow, steady, rarely reactive to short-term news
Retail investors
Individuals trading directly through brokers
News, price momentum, and personal cash flows
Highly variable; often buys enthusiastically after long rallies
Promoters
Founding families and parent companies
Control, strategy, occasionally personal liquidity
Rarely trade; when they sell large stakes, the market pays attention

body.label: Every Sale Has a Buyer
body.context: A headline saying foreigners sold ₹8,000 crore also means someone bought ₹8,000 crore. Price falls only if sellers are more impatient than buyers, which is why net flows across all groups tell you more than any single number.

body.title: Do the Netting
body.prompt: On one day, FPIs sell ₹12,000 crore of Indian equities while domestic institutions buy ₹14,500 crore. What is the net institutional flow, in ₹ crore? Use a minus sign if it is negative.
body.explanation: ₹14,500 crore minus ₹12,000 crore is a net inflow of ₹2,500 crore. A headline that mentions only the foreign selling makes the day sound alarming, while the market may have closed higher. Always read both columns together.

body.title: Foreign Selling Absorbed by Domestic Buying (Illustrative Six Months)

body.text: The single biggest structural change in Indian markets over the last decade is that domestic money, arriving every month through SIPs, EPF and NPS, now regularly absorbs foreign selling. Indian markets are less at the mercy of global fund flows than they were a generation ago.

body.title: Why Foreign and Domestic Money Behave Differently

columns.label: Foreign Portfolio Money
points: Decisions are made comparing India against dozens of other markets
A rise in US interest rates can trigger selling in India with no Indian trigger at all
Currency matters: returns are earned in rupees but measured in dollars
Can exit fast, because mandates and risk limits force quick action
Concentrated in large, liquid stocks that can absorb big orders

columns.label: Domestic SIP and Retirement Money
points: Arrives on a fixed date every month, largely regardless of market level
Driven by household savings habits, not by global rate decisions
Measured in rupees, so currency moves are irrelevant to the investor
Slow to exit, because it is tied to long-term goals and payroll deductions
Spreads across mid and small caps too, which changes which stocks get bid up

body.title: Why Foreign Investors Sell India When Nothing Has Changed in India

children.text: Four reasons, and only the last is about India:
If safe US government bonds start paying meaningfully more, the case for taking emerging market risk weakens for every global allocator at once. This is the link back to Chapter 3.
A fund earning rupee returns but reporting in dollars loses part of its gain when the rupee weakens, so a strong dollar phase reduces appetite for Indian assets regardless of company performance.

A fund facing redemptions or losses in another market often sells its most liquid holdings to raise cash, and those tend to be large Indian stocks. Your employer's share price can fall because of a problem on another continent.
Valuations looking expensive against other emerging markets, a policy or tax change, or disappointing earnings. This is the only category where the answer lies at home.

body.title: The Currency Connection
body.question: Foreign investors sell a large quantity of Indian shares and take the money home. Ignoring RBI intervention, what does that do to the rupee?
options: Nothing, since share sales and currency markets are separate
The rupee weakens, because they sell rupees to buy dollars
The rupee strengthens, because Indian markets get cheaper
It depends only on the trade deficit
body.explanation: To repatriate money they must convert rupees into dollars, which increases demand for dollars and pressures the rupee. This is why heavy foreign selling often shows up as a weaker rupee on the same day, and why the equity and currency markets cannot be read in isolation.

body.text: Foreign selling is not a verdict on your employer. A global fund trimming its India allocation from 4% to 3% will sell a slice of every large holding, including well-run companies that just reported record results. Reading flow-driven price moves as a judgement on management is a mistake that gets made in boardrooms as often as in WhatsApp groups.

children.text: How Domestic Money Became the Counterweight

body.title: The Rise of the Indian Retail Investor

events.title: Foreign Flows Set the Tone
events.description: Indian equity markets were heavily dependent on foreign portfolio flows. When global funds turned sellers, there was limited domestic money to absorb it.

events.title: SIPs Go Mainstream
events.description: Systematic investment plans turned equity investing into a monthly payroll-linked habit for salaried households, creating a predictable flow of money into funds.

events.title: Retirement Money Enters Equity
events.description: EPFO began investing a portion of incremental contributions through equity index funds, and NPS equity allocations grew, adding a slow but very large domestic buyer.

events.title: Direct Participation Surges
events.description: Low-cost digital brokers and smartphone access brought a wave of first-time investors and a sharp rise in demat accounts.

events.title: Two Engines, Not One
events.description: Foreign money still moves prices, but domestic institutional buying now regularly offsets it. Market falls driven purely by foreign selling tend to be shallower than they once were.

stats.label: SIP Contributions
stats.context: Tens of thousands of crores flow in every month through systematic plans, published by AMFI

stats.label: Retirement Flows
stats.context: EPF and NPS contributions arrive with every payroll cycle, whatever the market is doing

stats.label: Foreign Ownership
stats.context: FPIs hold a large share of free float in big companies, so their trades still move prices

body.caption: What Each Group Tends to Do in a Sharp Fall

cells: FPIs
Sell to reduce risk, often across all emerging markets at once
Amplifies the fall, particularly in large liquid stocks
Mutual funds
Keep buying as long as SIP money keeps arriving
Cushions the fall, unless investors stop their SIPs
Insurers and pension funds
Continue allocating to plan, sometimes buying more as prices fall
Stabilising, though slow to show up
Retail investors
Behaviour splits: some buy the dip, others stop SIPs at exactly the wrong time
Unpredictable, and a genuine risk to the domestic cushion
Promoters
Occasionally buy from the open market, which is a public signal of confidence
Small in volume, large in signalling value

body.text: The domestic cushion depends on ordinary savers continuing their monthly investments during a fall. If SIPs are paused en masse in a panic, the buying that absorbs foreign selling disappears exactly when it is most needed. The strength of this structural change is therefore a behavioural question, not a mechanical one.

body.title: The Board Wants to Know Why the Stock Fell
body.scenario: You support investor relations at a listed Indian company. Over three weeks the share price fell 14%, with no change in the business: the last quarterly results beat guidance, no customer was lost, and there is no pending litigation. Foreign investors were heavy net sellers of Indian equities across the same period, and your company has one of the higher foreign holdings in its sector. A board member asks whether the market has lost confidence in management.
body.prompt: How do you answer, with evidence, without either dismissing the fall or accepting blame that does not belong to the company?
body.modelAnswer: Answer with structure rather than reassurance. First, establish whether the fall was company-specific or market-wide by comparing the company against its sector index and against a broad index over the same three weeks; if peers with unrelated fundamentals fell similarly, the cause is largely external. Second, look at the ownership structure, because a company with high foreign ownership and high free float is mechanically more exposed when global funds reduce their India allocation, since they sell what they hold and what is liquid, not what is weak. Third, check the flow data for the period: if foreign investors were net sellers across Indian equities while domestic institutions absorbed part of it, that pattern is visible in published data and can be shown to the board directly. Fourth, examine whether anything structural changed in the shareholder register, such as a large holder exiting or an index weight adjustment, since both cause selling unrelated to performance. Having done that, the honest answer has two halves. On the evidence, this fall is consistent with a flow-driven and sector-wide move rather than a judgement on management, and the operating results support that reading. However, the board should not be told that price never matters: a sustained de-rating relative to peers would be a genuine signal, ESOP value and any future fundraising are affected, and if the company trades at a persistent discount to comparable businesses, the reasons deserve investigation. The recommendation is to track relative performance against sector peers over quarters rather than weeks, report the ownership concentration and flow context alongside the price, and resist both explanations offered in moments like this: that the market is simply wrong, and that the management is being judged.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Overseas funds registered with SEBI to invest in Indian securities are called foreign ___ investors.
body.explanation: Foreign portfolio investors, or FPIs, is the current term. News coverage often still says FIIs, which was the older designation, and the two are used interchangeably in practice.

body.title: How to Read Flow Data Without Being Misled
steps: Always read FPI and DII figures together, since one usually offsets part of the other
Check whether foreign selling was in the cash market or driven by derivatives positions, because the two say different things
Compare the size of the flow against typical monthly flows, so a routine number is not treated as a crisis
Look at the rupee on the same day, since repatriated money passes through the currency market
For a specific company, check foreign ownership levels, because a high holding means more sensitivity to global allocation changes
Ignore single-day figures when forming any view, and look at three to six month trends instead

body.label: AMFI: Mutual Fund and SIP Data
body.description: Monthly industry data on SIP contributions, net inflows by category and total assets under management. The clearest public evidence of how much domestic money is arriving in markets each month.

points: Four groups do most of the trading: foreign portfolio investors, domestic mutual funds, insurers and pension funds, retail investors, and occasionally promoters
Every sale has a buyer, so net flows across groups matter more than a dramatic figure for one of them
Foreign money reacts to global interest rates, the dollar and events in other markets, often selling India for reasons that have nothing to do with India
Domestic SIP, EPF and NPS money arrives every month regardless of market level, which now regularly absorbs foreign selling
Foreign selling forces rupee conversion, which is why heavy outflows and a weaker rupee often appear on the same day
Flow-driven price falls are not a verdict on a company's management, though a sustained relative de-rating is worth investigating
The domestic cushion holds only as long as ordinary savers keep investing during falls, which makes it a behavioural strength rather than a guaranteed one

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. All flow figures, price moves and time periods used are illustrative teaching examples rather than actual market data. Investor category definitions and disclosure requirements are set by SEBI and change over time, so refer to official sources such as SEBI, NSE, BSE and AMFI for current data and definitions.
